Short Summary: The Clarens Supply Store is one of the oldest commercial sites in the village, dating back to 1915. For over a century, this location has served as the primary trading hub for local farmers and residents. Originally, the site included a lean-to on the side of the building that functioned as a blacksmith's shop and small carpentry workshop, highlighting the store's role in the early agricultural economy.
Full History:
Historically, the store was a place of barter where farmers would exchange their crops for provisions. Mr. R. Sandler, a trader in the 1940s, was central to these exchanges. He owned the Supply Store from 1943 until Juan Frost took over in 1954, Over the years, the property underwent several consolidations, with Erf 420 and 520 merging into Erf 521 in 1990.

The store's history is populated by colourful local characters. During the 1970s, it was owned by Michael and Ruth Goldblatt and was known locally as "Masjoten" (the man with the short pants). In the 1980s, the store was run by Hans Oosthuizen, affectionately nicknamed "Matshwala" or "Mafikizolo" (the man who arrived yesterday) by the local community. His wife was known as "Maspeed" due to her thin build and quick pace.

The building has faced significant challenges, most notably in 1993 when it was badly damaged by a fire. Following the disaster, Riempies and Carla Claasen rented the property from Oosthuizen and oversaw its rebuilding. They restored the store and re-established it as a central retail point and petrol station, preserving its vital function for the town.

Today, the site continues to serve as the town's main grocery outlet, operating as Horeb Savemor. While the building has been modernized since the 1993 fire, it sits on the same historic foundations that have supported the commerce of Clarens since its founding years.
Key Facts: Built: 1915; Original function: Trading Store; First owner: Eduard C.D. Roos; Notable owners: R. Sandler (1943); Juan Frost (1954); Goldblatt family; Local nickname: Masjoten (Goldblatt era); Historic feature: Original blacksmith lean-to; Fire damage: 1993; Legendary clerk: "Mafikizolo" Hans Oosthuizen; Current business: Horeb Savemor

Street Address: Cnr Main and Van Zyl Streets, Clarens (Erven 354 & 360)
Short Summary: The building was a landmark sandstone residence with a rich history of both family life and commercial enterprise. Built in the 1930s by Mr. J. van Reenen, the house is famous for its exceptionally thick walls—more than half a meter of solid, locally hewn sandstone. A stoep was added later, wrapping around two sides of the original vintage structure.
Full History:
In the 1950s, the house was owned by Mr. J.C. Human, who operated a bakery from the premises. By the 1960s, the property had expanded its commercial footprint; a porch was added that encroached onto the municipal sidewalk, and a petrol pump was installed in front of what was then a small general shop. During this era, Main Street ran directly through what is now the Market Square.

The house returned to residential use for various periods, housing families such as the Van Zyls in the 1970s and Rev. Francois Brink in the mid-1980s. A major shift occurred in 1994 when the McRae family purchased the property. Recognising the growing tourism in the Eastern Free State, they transformed the residence into an information centre and coffee shop.

The name "Serendipity" was chosen to reflect the "facility of making happy chance discoveries," a fitting description for a town becoming a major tourist destination. The coffee shop became a local favourite, serving savoury and sweet crepes, pancakes, and light meals. It was considered a significant acquisition for the town's tourism infrastructure at the time.

In 1996, the property was purchased by Rob Crowther and Giel Lindeque as part of a larger plan to create the Clarens Meander Centre. Today, Serendipity House remains a key historical and commercial feature at the corner of Main and Van Zyl, its thick sandstone walls still standing as a testament to 1930s craftsmanship.

Walter Siviter started the Grouse and Claret Restaurant and Pub in 2000 and restored the building to its current state. After Walter passed away, his son Richard owned the Pub until 2025.

Rudo Schwimm and Rick Fryer took over the lease in 2025 and started the Firkin Pub and Grill, which is a popular music venue today.
Key Facts: First owner: Mr. J. van Reenen; Year built: ~1930s; Wall thickness: Over 50cm; Former use: Bakery (1950s); Notable owners: The McRae family; Meaning of name: "Happy chance discoveries"; Unique feature: Thick vintage sandstone walls; Historical detail: Former petrol pump site; Current use: Commercial/Meander Centre

Short Summary: President Square sits at the heart of Clarens, once serving as a central open veld where Main Road originally passed through. Today, the square is defined by its manicured layout and the prominent Naauwpoort Monument, which features a black granite plinth that replaced its original sandstone base.
Full History:
The square was established in 1912 as "Market Square" when the town was first laid out. The monument itself has a longer history, originally erected in 1896 on the farm Ararat to honour five burghers who died during an 1865 clash with Basotho warriors.

The battle occurred after a commando under Paul Kruger camped on the farm Ararat during a cold rainstorm. At three o'clock in the morning, Basotho warriors under Chiefs Lesoeana and Slanggaal launched a surprise attack on the un-laagered camp under the cover of darkness.

In 1962, during the town’s golden jubilee, the monument was dismantled and moved from the farm to the town square. At this time, the square was redesigned, the original main road was rerouted around it, and the area was renamed President Square in honour of Paul Kruger.

Today, the square and monument stand as the town’s most significant civic landmark. It remains a place of tribute and a primary gathering point for visitors exploring the historic centre of the village. In 2000 the square was named Clarens Square.
Key Facts: Original name: Market Square; Monument subject: Battle of Naauwpoort Nek; Date of battle: 29 September 1865; Commemorated: Five fallen burghers; Monument erected: 1896 (farm Ararat); Second unveiling: 9 November 1962; Unveiled by: State President C R Swart; Current name: Clarens Square

Short Summary: This charming sandstone building, currently known as "Die Spens," was originally built as a "dorpshuisie" or town house. Its construction is unique, featuring an outer shell of local sandstone blocks with an inner lining of raw clay bricks, providing excellent insulation against the Free State’s extreme temperatures.
Full History:
The cottage was built in 1931 by Florence de Leeuw, who had purchased the two erven that same year. For many decades, it served as a private residence. In 1992, the property was purchased by Bruce Weyer, who undertook significant renovations, including enlarging the structure and adding the iconic stoep that now wraps around the entire building.

During the early 2000s, the building transitioned from a residence into a vibrant commercial and artistic hub. It famously housed Clarens Interiors and Clarens Metal Works. It also served as a gallery space for prominent local artists, including the Gibson Mokhachane Gallery and works by Erika Turvey.

The property has maintained its artistic and heritage appeal through various changes in ownership. In 2015, it was acquired by Archar Brownlee, and it is currently owned by Julia Brownlee. Its location on the western edge of the market square makes it a prominent feature for visitors exploring the village centre.

Today, the building is a well-known stop for tourists and locals alike. It hosts a delectable delicatessen "Die Spens". While its function has shifted from a simple cottage to a commercial space, its architectural integrity — particularly the original sandstone work and the added stoep — remains a highlight of Market Street West.
Key Facts: First owner: Florence de Leeuw; Year built: 1931; Construction material: Sandstone and clay brick; Wall composition: Raw clay inner bricks; Architectural feature: Wrap-around stoep; Former business: Clarens Interiors; Notable gallery: Gibson Mokhachane Gallery; Current owner: Julia Brownlee; Current name: Die Spens

Short Summary: This small, two-room sandstone building stands as a cornerstone of Clarens’ civic history. Built from locally hewn sandstone, it was originally erected to serve as the very first municipal office for the newly formed village. Its simple, sturdy design reflected the practical needs of the local government during the town’s early years.
Full History:
The site was initially held by the Government Council Trust in 1913 before being formally handed over to the Municipality in 1919. For nearly five decades, it was the administrative heart of the town. In 1965, the municipality moved to its current, larger premises, and this small sandstone building began its long association with the village library.

Before moving into this building, the library was housed in a corrugated iron and wood structure on the corner of Main and Naude Streets. Once relocated to the sandstone office, it was managed by a dedicated Library Committee, including notable residents like Ray Morgan, Mrs. van Zyl, and Mike Goldblatt.

Helen Pretorius is perhaps the most well-known figure associated with the library, having run it for 23 years starting in 1985. During her tenure, the library became part of the Regional Library scheme, ensuring a rotating stock of fresh books for the community.

The building subsequently served as the Clarens Museum and information centre. Today, it houses the Community Arts and Crafts project, where local artists display traditional basketry and wrought iron work. It remains a beloved landmark on the town square, representing over a century of community service.
Key Facts: Primary material: Sandstone; Original function: First Municipal Office; Government handover: 1919; Library use: Moved here in 1965; Notable librarian: Helen Pretorius (1985–2008); Current function: Arts & Crafts Project; Structure size: Two-room building; Museum era: Used as Clarens Museum

Short Summary: The Ou Slaghuis (The Old Butchery) is a striking example of Clarens's vernacular architecture, featuring thick sandstone walls and a corrugated iron roof. The building occupies a large stand on Van Zyl Street, reflecting the sturdy construction methods used to serve the early farming community. While the property has evolved, the exterior retains its historical character, including a decorated front door and original sandstone pillars. It stands as one of the original commercial buildings constructed in the village's early years.
Full History:
The origins of the structure date back to the initial settlement of Clarens. Hermanus Pieters purchased the land in 1920 for fifty pounds, and local accounts suggest the building was constructed between 1920 and 1925. The construction is often attributed to the builder Gert van Zyl. As a village butchery, the site provided essential infrastructure in an era before refrigeration, making it a central hub for daily life alongside the post office.

For many years, the building was operated by local farmer Willy van Biljon, who was well-known for being one of the few residents to own a car. In the days before modern marketing, he would drive into town and send an employee running through the streets to announce the butchery was open for business. A specific window remains on one side of the building where Black residents were served, providing a physical record of the social history of that era.

The property remained within the Pieters family for decades, passing from Hermanus (who died in 1943) to his son H.B. Pieters and eventually to his grandchildren, David and Aletta, in 1978. Ownership then transitioned through Johan van Rensburg in 1984, A.T. Hartwig in 1990, Anmarie Mikula in 1991, and Quantum Leap Investments in 2001. After being owned by Pat van den Heever, the site was purchased in 2007 by artist Neil Moss and Mary Lane Moss, who transformed the sandstone structure into an art gallery.

Today, the Ou Slaghuis stands as a reminder of the working commercial fabric that defined early Clarens. Though it is now private property and must be appreciated from the street only, it remains a cornerstone of the village's architectural and social history. The Clarens Heritage Association continues to gather oral histories and archival material to preserve the full story of this sandstone landmark for future generations.
Key Facts: Built: c. 1920 – 1925; Materials: Sandstone, corrugated iron roof; Original use: Village butchery; First owner: Hermanus Pieters; Possible builder: Gert van Zyl; Notable feature: Original service window; Property size: 3011 square meters; Current use: Private property and gallery

Short Summary: One of Clarens’s most beloved landmarks, Clementines Restaurant stands on the corner of Church and Van Reenen Streets in what was originally a South African Railways bus maintenance shed — a corrugated iron structure complete with an inspection pit and a trap door for servicing the buses underneath.
Full History:
In 1992 Bruce Weyers acquired the old shed, and Jenny Roberts established Clarens Weavers there, giving the industrial space its first creative life. In 1997 Hugo and Anette Vyfer purchased the property, demolished the original shed, and redesigned it as The Buffalo Restaurant, which was run by Marie Verster.

In 1999 Wolfgang and Annie Bittner leased the building and opened a restaurant they named Clementines — a name that would become synonymous with fine dining in the village. They eventually purchased the property in 2003, and Wolfgang made further modifications to the front facade while retaining the building’s distinctive corrugated iron character. Tragedy struck when Annie died in a car accident, and Wolfgang gradually lost interest in the business.

In 2010 Shelley Tresidder (Horton) bought Clementines and has owned and run it ever since, continuing the tradition of exceptional food within the atmospheric iron-roofed dining room. Her husband Mark Horton joined the business in 2015. Today Clementines is as well known for its architecture as for its menu — the corrugated iron walls that once sheltered buses and mechanics now enclose one of the Free State’s most celebrated restaurants.
Key Facts: Original use: SA Railways bus maintenance shed; Inspection pit: Original feature — trap door for bus servicing; First reuse: 1992 — Bruce Weyers; Clarens Weavers (Jenny Roberts); Demolished & rebuilt: 1997 — Hugo & Anette Vyfer; The Buffalo Restaurant; Clementines opened: 1999 — Wolfgang & Annie Bittner (lease); Building purchased: 2003 — Wolfgang Bittner; Current owner: Shelley Tresidder (since 2010); Mark Horton joined: 2015; Structure: Corrugated iron retained from 1997 rebuild

Short Summary: This historic railway building is characterised by its massive Oregon pine sliding doors and a loading bank used for heavy freight. The property still preserves its original waiting room and restrooms at the rear of the lot.
Full History:
Established as a hub for the South African Railways (SAR & H) bus service, this site served as the primary link between Clarens and the Bethlehem train station. The bus was a lifeline for the town, bringing in passengers, post, supplies, and farm implements twice weekly.

For many years, the depot was managed by Daniel "Daan" Burger, who offloaded parcels and milk cans. Local legend holds that Daan was often accompanied by a ghost on his short daily walk from his home on Van Zyl Street to the depot.

After the bus service ceased, the building found new life in the 1990s as a bookshop called Bibliophile, which later moved to the adjacent property. The old ticket office was eventually converted into a kitchen to facilitate the building’s next transformation.

Today, the goods shed functions as the dining hall for "The Platform" restaurant. It stands as a well-preserved example of early 20th-century transport infrastructure, continuing to serve as a gathering place for the community.
Key Facts: Original function: Bus stop and loading bank; Operating entity: SAR & H (Railway); Service frequency: Twice a week; Ticket cost: 25 cents; Key feature: Oregon pine sliding doors; Current use: The Platform restaurant

Short Summary: On erven 311 and 312 along Church Street stands one of Clarens’s earliest surviving houses, built around 1918 — just a few years after the village was proclaimed in 1912, when the first settlers were still establishing a community in this remote highland valley.
Full History:
The house was originally associated with Sagonsky and Sandler, passing shortly afterwards to Harry Sandler alone. It was built with care and local materials: a sandstone foundation, walls of coursed rubble plastered with clay in the traditional manner of the early Eastern Free State, with Oregon pine floors and ceilings throughout the interior.

In 1996, Debra and Ken Stewart purchased the property and set about giving it new purpose. They also hired the derelict bus depot of SAS&H / SAR nearby and established a bookshop there — a modest beginning for what would become one of Clarens’s most beloved institutions.

After Ken Stewart’s death, Debra moved the bookshop onto the property itself. She had a new bookshop building erected using corrugated iron sheets salvaged from the original sheep shed of the farm Cornelia — an eclectic, characterful structure that visitors often describe as reminiscent of Pilgrim’s Rest.

The original house still stands on the property, its Oregon pine floors, ceilings and inner walls preserved much as they were a century ago. The property also retains a large orchard of old and rare apple varieties, an old wagon house, and corrugated iron shed at the back — quiet remnants of the property’s rural past. Together the house, the bookshop, the sandstone wall and the old orchard tell a story of continuity and reinvention.
Key Facts: First owners: Sagonsky & Sandler (1915); Harry Sandler (1917); Notable early owner: Corlia Roos (1946); Notable later owner: Panagiotus Aligianis (1991); Restored & repurposed: Debra & Ken Stewart (from 1996); Construction: Sandstone foundation, coursed rubble walls plastered with clay; Oregon pine floors and ceilings; Bookshop building: Red corrugated iron, from original sheep shed of farm Cornelia; Perimeter wall: Sandstone from Lake Clarens renovation (Marius Naudé’s farms)

Short Summary: Frost House at 264 Church Street is one of only two remaining corrugated iron buildings in Clarens still standing and occupied. Architect Jaap Boonstra believed it may originally have been a Victorian flat-pack structure built in the early 1920s — no original council plans survive to confirm the exact date.
Full History:
The Deeds Registry records a succession of owners: Van der Merwe (1914), Naude (1926), Luyt (1949), before Juan Max "Jack" Frost acquired it in 1974. Jack — a WWII RAF veteran, former racing car driver, and owner of the Clarens supply store — gave the house his name. He served on the Clarens Town Council and as deacon of the DR Church. By 1978, when artist Annetjie Muller sketched the house, it was still well maintained. After Jack sold in 1980 it passed through several hands and fell into serious disrepair.

In 2015 Adrian Smallpeice and Richard Pender bought the house with the specific aim of rescuing it from ruin. Working with architect Jaap Boonstra, they removed only two internal walls and retained the original timber windows, wooden floors, and vaulted ceilings. The footprint remains almost unchanged apart from a patio at the back.

The original wooden floor — nearly a century old — survived the years of neglect largely undamaged. The owners insisted that the builder Jacques Viljoen not sand it down, preserving its extraordinary patina. The village butcher "Riempies" donated the doorbell. The late Helen Boucher, a local farmer, designed the garden using grasses and plants transplanted from her farm wetland, with an indigenous hedgerow connecting the house to the surrounding landscape.
Key Facts: Address: 264 Church Street, Clarens; Built: ~Early 1920s (exact date unrecorded); Style: Victorian corrugated iron; Notable owner: Juan "Jack" Max Frost (1974-1980); Restoration: 2015 — Smallpeice & Pender; Architect: Jaap Boonstra; Status: Section 38, NHRA

Short Summary: Standing on Main Street, on erven 281 and 282, the building known today as The Maze is one of the oldest surviving structures in Clarens. It was built around 1912 — the very year the village was proclaimed — making it a true founding building of the town. Unusually for Clarens, where local sandstone became the dominant building material, the original house was constructed of corrugated iron, a reminder that the first settlers used whatever materials they could transport into this remote highland valley.
Full History:
The house was the home of the Fischer family, with Maria Elizabeth Fischer recorded as owner from 1915. In those earliest years it also served as the rectory of the Dutch Reformed Church, housing Clarens’s first DRC minister, Rev. P.J. Stander. As the village grew, Mrs Fischer converted it into a boarding house and added a large kitchen.

The Fischer family retained the property until 1929, when it passed through a series of owners. In 1966 the property was acquired by Ruth Goldblatt, who set it up as a café and tearoom. During the 1980s the building served as the local offices of the Conservative Party. By 1990 it had returned to hospitality as the Guinea Feather restaurant.

It was saved from demolition in 1994 when Bruce Weyer purchased it and undertook a substantial restoration and expansion, bringing the total footprint to 440 m². Weyer added a new stoep with traditional brokie lace decorative ironwork. The restored complex became home to the Clarens Weavers craft collective, and later the Street Caffé, run by Carl Swerts.

The building now operates as The Maze, a collection of small local shops. Through all its incarnations — rectory, boarding house, tearoom, party offices, restaurant, gallery, café — the original core of the 1912 Fischer house has endured. The original wooden floors, ceilings, and inner walls remain visible inside, a quiet and tangible link to the very founding of Clarens.
Key Facts: First owner/builder: Fischer, Maria Elizabeth (deeds from 1915; built c. 1912); Original function: Private residence / DRC rectory; First DRC Minister: Rev. P.J. Stander; Early use: Boarding house (Mrs Fischer); Construction type: Corrugated iron — rare in sandstone-dominant Clarens; Key restoration: Bruce Weyer (purchased 1994, extended to 440 m²); Notable interior: Original wooden floors, ceilings and inner walls still intact; Current use: The Maze — collection of small shops

Short Summary: The Posthouse is a famous sandstone landmark located near the corner of Main and Naude Streets. Its design reflects its history as a central public utility, once featuring post boxes on its wide stoep and a manual telephone exchange room at the back.
Full History:
Built by the De Leeuw family in 1926, the building was immediately leased to the provincial government to serve as Clarens’ primary post office. It became the central pulse of the village, where the daily bus dropped off parcels and mail for all the locals to collect.

The building’s early history was dominated by Louisa Liddell, a strict postmistress who managed the counter, the local news, and the telephone exchange simultaneously. Residents who forgot their post box keys would often receive a reprimand before she would assist them.

In 1992, the building was purchased by Bruce Weyers, but a rental dispute eventually led to the post office’s closure and relocation in 1993. In 1998, Bruce and Debbie Marx bought the property and performed a sensitive restoration using stones from an old farm Beginsel to convert it into a restaurant.

The building remains one of the most beautiful and well-known structures in Clarens. It continues to operate as a restaurant, preserving its historic character while serving as a popular destination for both locals and tourists.
Key Facts: Original builders: The De Leeuw family; Year built: 1926; Initial use: Provincial government post office; First postmistress: Louisa Liddell; Telephone service: National grid arrived late 1980s; Post office closed: 1993 (relocation); Restoration date: 1998; Restoration material: Re-used farm house stone; Current use: Restaurant

Short Summary: The Dutch Reformed congregation of Clarens was established in 1920 and Ds Stander was the first minister. Bethlehem itinerant ministers held services for the farming community in the Holkrans on "Ouwerf" before and during the Anglo-Boer War. After the town Clarens was established in 1912, the Bethlehem ministers built a little corrugated iron church as a "buitekerk" on the corner of Main and Naude Streets and services were held there from February 1914 till 1941.
Full History:
The erven for the new church was donated by J van Straaten. Though initially the church council requested the Louwe and Moerdyk firm to draw plans, they found it too costly and accepted Ds J J le Roux's plans and laid the foundation stone in February 1940. Both Gert van Zyls were the stonemasons. The tower was capped with a copper Swiss style onion-shaped dome which was later replaced by an extended tower with a clock, bell and a weather cock. Inside the church boasts a Moller organ, wooden pews and pulpit.

The sandstone church on the church square, finally inaugurated on 6 February 1941, more than two decades after the congregation was founded, reflected the practical realities of a small rural community raising its own funds. When it finally rose from the ground in local sandstone, it gave the church square the architectural anchor it still has today.

The church and the adjacent Gerhard Moerdyk Parsonage are both national monuments, proudly maintained by the congregation. Together they represent over a century of Dutch Reformed community life in Clarens.
Key Facts: Congregation founded: 1920; First services: Ministers from Bethlehem (Holkrans); First church: Corrugated iron — cnr Main and Naude Streets; Church built: Feb 1941; Architect: Ds J J le Roux; Status: National Monument

Short Summary: One cold winter night in the early 1920s, a rising young architect named Gerhard Moerdyk visited his friend Rev. SJ Stander in Clarens. They slept in the congregation’s first parsonage — a draughty corrugated iron house opposite the Post Office — and nearly froze. The next morning Moerdyk made a promise: he would design a proper home for the minister.
Full History:
The result, completed in 1923, was a stately sandstone parsonage on a plot donated by Mr D van Zyl. Moerdyk’s firm Moerdyk & Louw drew the plans; brothers Prinsloo and Naude built it; and Mr Keyter, a member of the Volksraad, provided the loan that made it possible. Moerdyk would go on to design the Voortrekker Monument in Pretoria — making his connection to this modest village an extraordinary footnote in South African architectural history.

In the 1980s, rising maintenance costs led the church council to consider selling the building. A local architect and congregation member stepped in, redesigning the interior and adding a roof space with a staircase that made the house significantly warmer and more practical. The building was saved.

In 2020 the church council completed a full restoration, returning the parsonage to its former glory. It is a national monument — and a reminder that great architecture sometimes begins with a freezing cold night and a generous promise.
Key Facts: Built: 1923; Architect: Gerhard Moerdyk (1890–1950); Firm: Moerdyk & Louw; Builder: Brothers Prinsloo & Naude; Plot donated by: Mr D van Zyl; Financed by: Mr Keyter, Volksraad member; Restored: 2020 (church council); Status: National Monument

Short Summary: The Ou Kliphuis — Erven 177 and 178 on Main Street, opposite the Church Hall — is a typical small one-bedroom sandstone house, built around 1927 according to former Clarens mayor Martie Lotz, though no original Deeds Office records confirm the exact date. It likely served as a dorpshuisie for farming families attending nagmaal and church.
Full History:
In the late 1950s, (Awat) Eduard Christiaan Daniel Bruwer (1905–1979) and his half-sister Elsje van Zyl (1898–1966) bought the house — nicknamed “Saal-maar-af.” Bruwer was born on the nearby farm Beginsel and had deep ties to Clarens. The family kept it as a holiday home for more than thirty years; in 1970 the house still had no electricity.

In 1990, Rika Susanna Raats (daughter of E C D Bruwer) became owner. Erven 177 measured 798 m², valued at R7 500, with the house at R11 400. She did sensitive restoration around 2000, maintaining the absence of electricity and the Dover coal stove in the small kitchen.

In 2014, Nancy Whittaker’s daughter Oonagh Wohanka purchased the house. Architect Jaap Boonstra drew the renovation plans and Bruce Marx was the builder. The kitchen, scullery, and en-suite bedrooms were extended; a new gable was constructed using repurposed sandstone from Beginsel farm to mirror the original. Only three doors, four windows, and the front sandstone façade remain unchanged.

Nancy Whittaker — artist, writer, chef, and enthusiastic gardener — lived in the house until her death in 2022, creating the beautiful cottage garden still enjoyed today. Her son Bruce Fordyce, the celebrated South African marathon runner, has close ties with Clarens. The family continues to own and operate Ou Kliphuis as a guest house.
Key Facts: Built: ~1927 (no original records); Erven: 177 & 178, Main Street; Material: Sandstone; Original use: Nagmaal dorpshuisie; Architect (2013–14): Jaap Boonstra; Builder (2013–14): Bruce Marx; Current use: Guest house; Status: Section 34(1), NHRA (60+ years)

Short Summary: The Kruger Gedenksaal, later known as the N.G. Kerksaal, has long been a centre for community life in Clarens. It was originally erected in 1921 by the Oranje Vroue Vereniging (OVV), a prominent women's organisation. From its inception, the hall served as a versatile venue for the village, hosting everything from formal concerts to early film screenings.
Full History:
The building has always maintained a strong spiritual and social connection with the Nederduitse Gereformeerde (NG) Church. However, it was only in 1952 that the church council officially purchased the hall from the OVV. Following the purchase, it became the primary hall for church functions and community gatherings.

An interesting chapter in the building's history involved the church council operating a restaurant from the premises. This reflected the hall's central location on the Plein and its role as a gathering place for both locals and the early travellers visiting the scenic Maluti mountains.

As the town grew, the hall continued to be the primary indoor space for large public events. Its proximity to the Clarens Plein and the main commercial street ensured it remained a focal point of village activity. The hall's simple but dignified architecture is typical of early 20th-century community buildings in the Free State.

Today, the hall continues to serve the NG Church and the broader Clarens community. While its days as a cinema and a church-run restaurant have passed, its significance as a heritage site lies in its century-long role as the "living room" of the village.
Key Facts: Built by: OVV (Oranje Vroue Vereniging); Year: 1921; Original use: Concerts and films; Historical name: Kruger Gedenksaal; Acquired by NG Church: 1952; Church role: Church Hall; Former feature: Church-run restaurant, kitchen and offices; Significance: Strong community/church link

Short Summary: The Methodist Church on the corner of Roos and Bester Streets is one of the most cherished buildings in Clarens. The first Methodist services in the district were held as far back as 1866, when Joseph Liddell — a Scottish missionary at Bethel farm — conducted services for English, Scottish, and Irish farming families along the Basotho border, long before any town existed.
Full History:
For decades the English-speaking community gathered at St Fort (the Walker homestead), at Dunblane, and later in Classroom No. 3 of Clarens Primary School. Ministers from Bethlehem travelled five hours by gig or horseback each month to conduct Holy Communion.

In 1936 the community finally built its own church. The Clarens Council donated the erven; James Strapp of Bethlehem paid off the Bethlehem church debt, and that congregation donated 650 pounds to Clarens. The Liddell brothers carted sandstone from their farms by ox-wagon; Gert van Zyl was the stonemason; Hugo Walker crafted every pew, beam, and fitting by hand — losing three fingers in the process.

Emma Walker of St Fort laid the cornerstone on 3 August 1936, sealing coins, a newspaper, and magazines beneath it. On opening day the final 40 pounds was raised on the spot. Today the building is almost entirely unaltered — original beams, pews, wooden floor, and stained-glass windows all in place. Hugo also crafted the pulpit, completing a remarkable contribution to the building. Memorials to the Liddell brothers and Hugo Walker are mounted on the walls.

The organ, faithfully pumped by Harry Mokoena for many years, now stands in the church hall. The first permanent minister of the congregation was Francois Brink.
Key Facts: First services: 1866 (Joseph Liddell, Bethel farm); Cornerstone laid: 3 August 1936; Total cost: 650 pounds; Donor: Bethlehem Methodist Church; Stone from: Liddell & Walker families; Carpenter: Hugo Walker (lost three fingers); Pulpit: Crafted by Hugo Walker; Organ: Pumped by Harry Mokoena; now in church hall; First permanent minister: Francois Brink; Status: Section 38, NHRA

Short Summary: In 1914 a new three-classroom sandstone school was built on the corner of Main and Malherbe Streets, with stone hewn from the quarry near Kgubetswana. The townspeople quarried, loaded, and delivered the sandstone blocks by ox-wagon for months. Skilled stonemasons laid the foundations and walls; carpenters fitted the roof, ceilings, sash windows, and wooden doors. At the back were two washing rooms with four basins each. Every classroom was heated by a Queen coal stove.
Full History:
On 24 August 1914, principal Mr J.S. de Leeuw wrote in the School Journal: "Duties were taken up in the new school building and five more pupils admitted." On 2 September 1914, H. de Villiers — Chairman of the Bethlehem School Board — officially opened the Clarens School with 42 pupils on the roll.

Jimmy de Leeuw served as principal from 1914 to 1944 — thirty years at the helm of the school he helped open. His steady leadership shaped the educational character of the village through its earliest and most formative decades.

The original sash windows were replaced with steel windows in 1968. During the 2014 renovation the sandstone building was retained and carefully converted into school offices using reversible dry-walling, preserving its full heritage value. From 42 founding pupils the school now serves over 1,000 learners.
Key Facts: Built: 1914; Material: Sandstone (Kgubetswana quarry); First principal: J.S. (Jimmy) de Leeuw (1914–1944); Opening: 2 September 1914 — 42 pupils; Windows: Sash replaced 1968; renovated 2014; Current use: School administration offices; Status: Section 38, NHRA

Street Address: Erf No. 1, Cnr Steyn and Hill Streets
Short Summary: Leliehoek house sits on a large property at the corner of Steyn and Hill Streets. It was once the centre of a significant farm that eventually provided the land upon which the town of Clarens was established.
Full History:
The house was likely built between 1893 and 1900, as it does not appear on earlier farm maps. It was the homestead of Hermanus Hendrik Steyn and his wife Jacoba de Villiers (oldest daughter of PH de Villiers), who inherited the land when the original Naauwpoortsnek farm was divided among seven children in 1907.

In 1910, Steyn sold the farm to the Clarens Promoting Society Company and moved to Kenya due to his dissatisfaction with the British takeover after the Anglo-Boer War. From 1915 to 1919 the house was owned by Jim van Zyl, a general dealer who owned a shop on the property where the Post House is today. Subsequent residents included George Johnston, the brother of local mayor Florence de Leeuw, who lived there for over thirty years.

The property underwent significant change in 1980 when it was inherited by Kristy Leybrandt and her husband Richard Thomas. They subdivided the large three-morgen plot into eleven smaller erven, fundamentally changing the original setting of the old homestead.

A sturdy sandstone house with minimum alterations throughout the years is still standing proudly showing off the excellent craftsmanship of stone masons in stone cutting, texture and craftsmanship of sandstone construction, early building traditions and distinctive vernacular architecture rooted in local conditions around the turn of the 20th century and the intimate detail of this family house which had been well preserved, maintained and is still in reuse with continued relevance acting as a guest house in the modern scope of Clarens as a tourist hub.
Key Facts: Farm origin: Naauwpoortsnek partition — Leliehoek farm no 1203, 429 morgen; Stand size: Original 429 morgen; after town founding a plot of three morgen; First owner: Hermanus Hendrik Steyn; Former residents: Jim van Zyl, George Johnston, the Leibrandts; Sale date: 1910 to the Clarens Promoting Society Company; Current status: Divided into 11 erven with original homestead on 16/1

Short Summary: Sutherlands Cottage is a classic example of early Clarens sandstone architecture, characterized by its thick, 600mm inner walls and sturdy construction. The original layout was modest, featuring a 4x4m voorkamer (living room) with two small bedrooms leading from it, a small kitchen, and an outside ablution. A prominent open stoep originally graced the front of the house.
Full History:
According to local history, the house was built in July 1906 for the Heidenrich family. The patriarch, old man Heidenrich, was known for sitting on the front stoep to watch the sunset with a "tippie". While early records suggest the roof was originally thatch during the 1920s, this has been contested by some deeds office records.

In 1922 Manie Pieterse, who owned "die Ou Slaghuis", bought the property and owned it until 1934.

There was several owners until 1953, when the property was purchased by Daniel Ignatius "Daan" Burger, who worked at the local Railway depot. Daan was responsible for offloading post, milk cans, and passengers from the buses. Local legend from the Burger family suggests that Daan was often accompanied by a "ghost" on his short daily walk from the house to the depot.

Under the Burger family’s ownership, an additional room was added for the children, which now serves as a large lounge area. The property changed hands several times in the late 20th century, notably being owned by Robert Bruce Sutherland in 1989, from whom the name "Sutherlands Cottage" originated. Later, artist Veronica Mary (Vee) Tiley resided there, initially living in a treehouse at the bottom of the garden.

Today, the cottage remains a significant heritage site on Van Zyl Street, preserved as a private residence. Its thick sandstone walls and historical proportions continue to reflect the early building styles of the region.
Key Facts: Original owner: Heidenrich family; Construction material: Sandstone blocks; Wall thickness: 600mm; Roof type: Original thatch (now corrugated iron); Notable resident: Daniel Ignatius (Daan) Burger; Former name: Sutherlands Cottage; Historical use: Residential; Current use: Artist residence and garden

Short Summary: The home at 429 Berg Street is a charming example of early Clarens architecture, set on a 1983-square-meter erf. The heart of the current residence is the original lounge, which once constituted the entire footprint of the first small cottage. Over the decades, the property has evolved from a simple stone structure into a refined residence, recently redesigned and restored to preserve its historical character while integrating modern architectural elements.
Full History:
Construction of the original dwelling dates back to 1895, under the ownership of Pieter Joshua Brandt. This early structure was a modest 6 by 8 square meters, typical of the era's standard. In 1913, an extension was added by the Van der Merwe family, a change marked by a surviving inscription above the stoep door.

The property is rich with personal history, particularly during the residence of the Steyn family in 1929. Johannes Steyn served as the local handyman and beadle for the Dutch Reformed Church, while his wife, Ansie, ran a "Tuisnywerheid" from the house. She was well-known in the community for selling homemade fudge, sweet milk cheese, and various artisanal cheeses. Memoirs from their daughter, Marti Lotz, even recall a baby's grave once tended in the front yard.

In later years, the site became a hub for the local art community. Between 1986 and 1999, it was home to artist and teacher Ann Rudnick, followed by Geertjie and Johan Kleingeld, who operated the Kethaba Art Studio where they produced batik designs and oil paintings.

In 2009, the Beukes family converted the property into a self-catering cottage known as "Vintage House," furnished with a distinct French flair. Following its 2024 restoration by architect Jacquie le Roux, it continues to stand as one of the most recognisable historic homes on Berg Street, a significant link to the village's founding families and its creative heritage.
Key Facts: Original owner: Pieter Joshua Brandt; First extension: 1913 by Van der Merwe; Original size: 6 x 8 square meters; Notable residents: Johannes and Ansie Steyn; Historic use: Home Industry (Tuisnywerheid); Recent name: Kethaba Art Studio; Current use: Self-catering cottage; Architect (2024): Jacquie le Roux

Short Summary: Berg Cottage is a distinctive L-shaped gabled house that stands as a testament to the resourcefulness of Clarens' early builders. The thick walls were constructed using traditional mud and stone, originally covered with wallpaper to prevent crumbling. Inside, the home features low doorways, wooden flooring in the primary rooms, and original roof trusses cut from local poplar trees that remain in place today.
Full History:
The house was likely built shortly after the village was proclaimed in 1912, with Nicolaas Albertus Smith listed as the owner by 1913. In its earliest form, it was a simple cottage consisting of a voorkamer, a kitchen, one bedroom, and an open stoep. The ceilings and cornices were fashioned from leftover planking and scrap wood, highlighting the modest origins of the structure.

Key transformations occurred under the ownership of Hendrik Grobbelaar (1948–1964) and Jannie van Wyk (1964–1981). Grobbelaar expanded the home to accommodate his growing family and built a shed next to the house where he serviced tractors and car engines—a building now known as the "Vine Shed." Jannie van Wyk renamed the home "Solitaire" and is credited with creating the lush garden, hand-building the terraces, and planting the vines and fruit trees that still characterize the property.

In 1981, Patsy and Peter Millen purchased the property after falling in love with its charm. They renamed it "Berg Cottage" and established Clarens' very first self-catering and bed-and-breakfast business. For years, it served as a welcoming base for hikers and climbers exploring the surrounding Maluti Mountains.

As of 2026, the house remains in the Millen family, owned by Patsy's daughters. It stands as a significant heritage site, not only for its unique mud-and-stone construction but for its role in pioneering the tourism industry that now defines the village of Clarens.
Key Facts: Original owner: Nicolaas Albertus Smith; Wall materials: Mud and stone; Roof trusses: Hand-cut poplar trees; Former name: Solitaire; Tourism milestone: First Clarens bed and breakfast; Original kitchen stove: Known as "Black Magic"; Outbuilding use: Former mechanical workshop (Vine Shed); Garden feature: Landscaped terraces and vine pergola

Short Summary: Located on the corner of Berg and Cilliers Streets, this house was originally built with hewn sandstone. In its earliest days, it was a modest two-room cottage with clay and cow-dung floors and a roof made of reeds and wood.
Full History:
Though deeds records show various owners like Philippus Steyl and Daniel van Zyl, the cottage is most famously associated with Jan de Jager. As his family grew, he partitioned the two large rooms into four by erecting internal walls.

Jan de Jager was a respected local blacksmith who shoed horses and repaired wagons and ploughs. He also operated a small mill near the village entrance powered by a Hornby Ruston engine. His life was marked by tragedy when his wife, Annie, died in 1934, leading to their children being sent to an orphanage.

Over time, the cottage’s primitive roof was replaced, first with corrugated iron and more recently with thatch. Modern extensions have added a kitchen, bathroom, and an extra bedroom to the historic structure.

Today, the property is owned by Yolanda van der Merwe, a teacher at the local primary school. The stand still features its original sandstone fence pillars and several old fruit trees, though a new house is being constructed on the corner of the property.
Key Facts: Original floors: Clay and cow dung; Original roof: Wood and reeds; Primary resident: Jan de Jager; Trade: Blacksmith and miller; Water source: Local well at Swart St; Current status: Residential home

Short Summary: Ou Werf lies on a broad, historic werf beneath the sandstone cliffs, overlooking the landscape toward Titanic Rock. The site includes remnants of early farm structures, a restored mud-and-clay school building, and a sandstone outbuilding. Nearby, the Holkrans cave forms a natural focal point, with stone kraals, scattered artefacts, and evidence of long human occupation embedded in the terrain.
Full History:
This is part of the original farm where Clarens originated before the establishment of the town. The location near Naauwpoort, an important entry route into the Caledon valley, was a natural point where early trade took place and where wagons entering the valley stopped to overnight. Church services were held in the holkrans (cave), a certain Mr Throllip had a shop and there was a blacksmith. Children went to school in the holkrans and later in a little mud hut that was erected for this purpose.

The origins of Ou Werf date to the farm Naauwpoortsnek, acquired around 1874 by Pieter de Villiers from his father-in-law, Jan Andries Kok. The farm was divided in 1907, and the portion that became Erf 490 passed to the youngest son, Basie de Villiers. In 1912, the land was sold to the Clarens Township Promoting Society, marking the transition from farmstead to part of the newly established town.

The werf played an important early role in community life. A simple two-room mud-and-reed structure served as the first government school for Clarens between 1913 and 1914. The site also functioned as a service hub for surrounding farms, with outbuildings, storage areas, and a nearby sandstone store. The Holkrans cave holds layered history, including San rock art, stone-age artefacts, and traces of later settler use such as church gatherings and livestock enclosures.

During the twentieth century, the property passed through several hands. It was associated with the Van Zyl family from the 1930s to about 1960, followed by sculptor Alfonso Smuts and his wife Nina, who lived and worked there from around 1960 to 1979. In this period, the original farmhouse was demolished and replaced with a barn built from its sandstone. From 1980, Maria Johanna Wessels occupied the property, and from 1989 her son, artist and musician Martin Wessels, lived there with Annetjie de Clercq, using the buildings and cave as creative spaces.

Today, Ou Werf remains one of the most historically layered sites in Clarens. The property is owned by Julie Brownlee, who inherited it in 2011 and has undertaken careful restoration. The old school building has been returned to residential use, while the sandstone barn has been converted into guest accommodation. The accommodation on the site is now known as "The French Cottage" and "Bungalow Belle Vie". The site continues to reveal artefacts from different eras, preserving a continuous record of settlement, adaptation, and cultural life in Clarens.
Key Facts: Original farm: Naauwpoortsnek; First owner: Pieter de Villiers (~1874); Earlier occupant: Jan Andries Kok; Farm division: 1907; Town formation: 1912; Later owners: Van Zyl, Smuts, Wessels; Key feature: Holkrans cave; Materials: Sandstone, mud, clay

Short Summary: This one of the oldest houses in Clarens. This heritage home occupies a prominent corner position at the intersection of Berg and Short Streets. It is immediately recognisable by its original perimeter fence, constructed from local sandstone with sturdy pillars and a vintage iron gate. The expansive garden is filled with historic fruit trees, including walnut, pear, and apple, typical of early Clarens residential plots.
Full History:
The house itself is a solid sandstone structure topped with a corrugated iron roof. The layout originally included a central room flanked by two bedrooms, a kitchen, and a front stoep. Over time, the stoep was enclosed and plastered to create additional indoor space, a common modification in the village’s colder climate.

The interior preserves several authentic early-20th-century elements. Three rooms still feature their original Oregon pine floors. Hidden within the roof space are raw poplar tree trunks used as support beams, a building technique used by early settlers when formal timber was scarce.

Architectural charm is added by the decorative woodwork throughout the home. The front door and bedroom doors are fitted with unique stained glass panels, and much of the original door hardware remains intact. While the kitchen has been modernised, the core of the house remains a tribute to traditional sandstone craftsmanship.

It remains a significant contributor to the heritage streetscape of the Swartland area.
Key Facts: Location: Corner of Berg/Short Streets; Property size: 3000+ m²; Early owners: 1919 — D J van den Berg; P L Steyl; Pieterse families (1946–1973); Exterior walls: Sandstone; Roofing: Corrugated iron; Floor type: Oregon pine; Ceiling structure: Original poplar beams; Decorative element: Stained glass panels; Landscaping: Mature fruit orchard

Street Address: Corner Steil Street & Naauwpoort Street, Erf 503
Short Summary: The building now known as Maluti Mountain Lodge has the longest hospitality history in Clarens. It began life as the Clarens Motel, constructed in the late 1950s on what is today erf 503 — across the spruit from the village centre, where the Country Lodge now also stands nearby.
Full History:
The motel was established by a local couple: an artist and school inspector, and his wife Jannie (J.A.J. van Wyk, née Janse van Rensburg / de Beer, born 1918). Because her husband could not hold a liquor licence, Jannie ran the establishment herself. For many years it was the only place in Clarens to sleep, eat, and have a drink — the essential stop for travellers between Golden Gate Highlands National Park and Bethlehem.

When her husband died tragically, Jannie lost her enthusiasm for the business and sold it in 1964 to Clarens Investments and new proprietors Bill and Jill Annandale, who continued to grow the flourishing establishment. Subsequent owners Ridley and Yvonne Rosensweig gave it its current name, carrying out significant renovations and refreshing the bar and lounge interiors.

In 1992 the property passed to the Janice and Julia Brownlee Trust, who operated it for nearly two decades until 2009. The current owner, Dan Lategan, has since expanded the accommodation with additional rondawels and a conference room at the rear, and has firmly positioned Maluti Mountain Lodge as a fly-fishing and biker-friendly destination.

Lategan himself is an enthusiastic motorcyclist, and the lodge is regarded as the premier bikers’ stop in the Eastern Free State. The lodge today draws its core clientele primarily from the biking community, as well as conferencing and fly-fishing visitors.
Key Facts: Original name: Clarens Motel; Builder/first owner: J.A.J. van Wyk (née Janse van Rensburg / de Beer, b. 1918); Notable operator: "Jannie" van Wyk (ran the bar after husband's death); Sold to: Clarens Investments / Bill & Jill Annandale (1964); Renamed by: Ridley & Yvonne Rosensweig; Managed by: Harry & Margaret Newton (for Rosensweigs); Sold 1992: Janice & Julia Brownlee Trust (ran until 2009); Current owner: Dan Lategan; Significance: Oldest continuously operating lodging in Clarens

Street Address: R711, approx. 2 km north of Clarens
Short Summary: About two kilometres north of Clarens on the R711, a dramatic natural sandstone formation rises from the landscape in a shape that has long reminded observers of the bow of a great ship cutting through water.
Full History:
The rock was named in 1912 — the same year Clarens was established and the same year RMS Titanic sank in the North Atlantic. Whether a deliberate tribute or a coincidence of timing, the double anniversary gives the formation a poignant resonance.

The Clarens Formation sandstone was laid down as desert dunes roughly 180 million years ago. The same distinctive amber and cream stone was later quarried by the founders to build the first houses, schools, and churches.

Titanic Rock is a reminder that the heritage of Clarens extends far beyond human history. The landscape itself — its cliffs, caves, and rock formations — shaped where and how people settled, and continues to define the village’s remarkable character.
Key Facts: Formed: ~180 million years ago; Named: 1912; Rock type: Clarens Formation sandstone; Location: ~2 km north on R711; Named for: Titanic disaster & town founding, both 1912

Short Summary: About eight kilometres from Clarens on the R711 towards Fouriesburg, the Schaapplaats rock art site is one of South Africa’s twelve declared Rock Art National Monuments, reached by a 2.7-kilometre walk along a stream.
Full History:
The shelter contains 35 images, including eight therianthropes — part-human, part-animal figures representing the shaman entering the spirit world during a trance dance.

Along the path visitors encounter additional heritage: a dinosaur footprint preserved in the rock, and a small graveyard from a British field hospital during the Anglo-Boer War (1899-1902).

Booking is essential and admission is R50 per person. Schaapplaats offers one of the most complete San art experiences in the Free State.
Key Facts: Age: ~2,000 years; Paintings: 35 images incl. 8 therianthropes; Status: National Monument; Hike: ~2.7 km along stream; Admission: R50 | Booking essential

Short Summary: In July 1900, British forces under General Archibald Hunter completed the encirclement of the Brandwater Basin, trapping the bulk of the Free State Boer forces in the mountain country near Fouriesburg. General Christiaan de Wet, escorting President Steyn, had already slipped out through Slabbert’s Nek on the night of 15 July with roughly 2,000 men — one of the most celebrated escapes of the entire war.
Full History:
Those left behind fell into confusion. On 27 July the Boers attempted to retreat along the Little Caledon River towards Golden Gate but were turned back by British forces under General Macdonald. They fell back to Slaapkrans — now known as Surrender Hill. On the night of 28 July the British seized the hill. Chief Commandant Marthinus Prinsloo, surrounded and unable to break out, surrendered unconditionally on 30 July 1900.

The total haul was staggering: 4,314 prisoners, three field guns, 2,800 head of cattle, and an estimated six million rounds of ammunition — all burnt on the hill by the British. It was the largest single surrender of Boer forces in the entire Anglo-Boer War — surpassing even Cronje’s surrender at Paardeberg.

The prisoners were transported by train to Cape Town and shipped to prisoner-of-war camps in Ceylon, Bermuda, and St Helena. They were permitted to return to South Africa only if they swore allegiance to the British Crown. Many refused and never returned. Christiaan de Wet, who had escaped, condemned the surrender as "’n gruwelike moord op regering, land en volk" — a horrible murder of government, country, and people.

Surrender Hill was declared a National Monument in 1986. A memorial marks the site, about 13 kilometres from Clarens on the R711 towards Fouriesburg. Parking is available 130 metres from the monument.
Key Facts: Original name: Slaapkrans / Verliesfontein; Date: 30 July 1900; Boers captured: 4,314 men, 3 field guns, 2,800 cattle; Ammo destroyed: ~6 million rounds (burnt on the hill); Commander: Chief Comdt. Marthinus Prinsloo; British general: Gen. Archibald Hunter; Notable escape: De Wet & Steyn — ~2,000 men via Slabbert’s Nek; POW destinations: Ceylon, Bermuda, St Helena; Status: National Monument (1986)

Street Address: Golden Gate Highlands NP, ~43 km from Clarens
Short Summary: The Basotho Cultural Village is a living open-air museum inside Golden Gate Highlands National Park, managed by SANParks. It presents Basotho homestead life from the 16th century to the present day through authentically reconstructed homesteads, each representing a different era. Resident guides demonstrate household implements, explain traditional clothing, and offer visitors the chance to meet the local chief and taste mqombothi — sorghum beer brewed on site.
Full History:
Three tours are on offer. The village tour runs seven days a week and takes 45 minutes. A two-hour herbal and rock art trail, offered Tuesdays to Thursdays, follows the village traditional healer through medicinal plant communities before continuing to a San rock art site. The full heritage programme — also Tuesdays to Thursdays — is a seven-hour immersive journey tracing the footsteps of the earliest inhabitants through the historical sites of QwaQwa.

The village has an art gallery, curio shop, and restaurant. Traditional crafts — pottery, beadwork, shweshwe textiles, and grass baskets — are produced and sold on site, supporting local artisans and the surrounding community.

Standing as a counterpoint to the Dutch-settler sandstone architecture of Clarens, the Basotho Cultural Village reminds visitors that the Maluti foothills have been home to many peoples across many centuries — long before the first wagons crossed the Rooiberge.
Key Facts: Managed by: SANParks; Location: Inside Golden Gate Highlands NP; Village tour: 7 days a week — 45 min; Herbal & rock art trail: Tue–Thu only — 2 hrs; Heritage programme: Tue–Thu only — 7 hrs; Admission: R60 (SA citizens) / R80 (foreign); Enquiries: +27 58 721 0300

Street Address: Golden Gate Highlands NP, ~15 km from Clarens
Short Summary: The Kgodumodumo Dinosaur Interpretive Centre opened in 2023 inside Golden Gate Highlands National Park. Designed by Mashabane Rose & Associates, its distinctive brickwork was patterned to evoke dinosaur scales.
Full History:
The centre interprets the world’s oldest known dinosaur nesting ground, uncovered here in 2012. The site contains nests, eggs, and footprints of Massospondylus — a prosauropod that walked these Jurassic floodplains between 190 and 225 million years ago.

Massospondylus footprints are preserved in the rock surfaces around the centre, allowing visitors to stand where ancient animals once walked. The discovery transformed understanding of dinosaur parental behaviour.

Paired with the Basotho Cultural Village and San rock art sites nearby, the Kgodumodumo Centre completes a remarkable timeline of life in this landscape.
Key Facts: Opened: 2023; Construction: 2019-2023; Architects: Mashabane Rose & Associates; Client: SANParks; Fossil site: World’s oldest known dinosaur nesting ground
